name: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)

lead: ACTH is the pituitary signal that tells your adrenal glands to make cortisol. Cortisol rhythm affects sleep, recovery, skin and where the body stores fat, which is why the topic appears in recovery and appearance discussions.

It comes from the same precursor as alpha-MSH, the peptide behind skin pigmentation. Medicinal versions such as Acthar Gel and cosyntropin are used by doctors for conditions like infantile spasms and adrenal testing.

paras: ACTH binds the MC2R receptor on adrenal cells, raising cAMP and driving cortisol and androgen production. Cortisol feeds back to the brain to lower further ACTH release.
Raising ACTH raises cortisol; extended exposure is associated with Cushing-type features such as weight gain, skin thinning and mood effects. It is a prescription-only product.

chain: ACTH signals the adrenals to make cortisol
Cortisol balance shapes sleep, recovery, skin and fat distribution
angle.text: People interested in recovery and skin look at ACTH because it sets the cortisol rhythm that affects sleep, training recovery and facial puffiness, and because it belongs to the same family as the melanocortins that darken skin. In practice it is a prescription hormone given by clinicians, and ACTH appears in appearance communities mainly as a lab value in hormone bloodwork.

lead: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH, corticotropin) is a 39-amino-acid hormone released by the anterior pituitary gland. It tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol and androgens and sits at the centre of the body's stress-response (HPA) axis.[1] It matters for appearance in three ways: cortisol balance influences sleep, recovery, fat distribution and skin; the same precursor molecule, POMC, also yields alpha-MSH, the signal that drives skin pigmentation; and ACTH-related blood tests are part of the work-up for hormone problems that change how the face and body look.[1][2][3]

ACTH acts through the melanocortin 2 receptor (MC2R), the only receptor for which it is the natural agonist, and the receptor needs a helper protein (MRAP) to reach the cell surface. Related melanocortin receptors respond to ACTH fragments and to alpha-MSH, which is why the very high ACTH of Addison's disease is accompanied by darker skin.[1][4]

Pharmaceutical corticotropin (marketed as Acthar Gel and in other forms) and the synthetic fragment tetracosactide (cosyntropin, Synacthen) are prescription products used by physicians, for example for infantile spasms and as a diagnostic test of adrenal function.[1][5] Registered clinical trials have studied it in nephrotic syndrome, multiple sclerosis, uveitis and rheumatoid arthritis.[6][7][8][9] Its use as a self-directed appearance aid is not described in the published literature.

paras: ACTH is cut from a 241-amino-acid precursor, proopiomelanocortin (POMC), which also produces alpha-MSH, CLIP, beta-lipotropin and beta-endorphin.[1] The hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone, which prompts pituitary corticotroph cells to secrete ACTH; cortisol then feeds back on both the hypothalamus and the pituitary, through a fast loop and a slower loop that lowers POMC gene transcription over hours to days.[1] The first 13 amino acids of ACTH make up alpha-MSH, and the whole molecule weighs about 4,540 daltons.[1]

ACTH is also tied to circadian rhythm. In laboratory stress research, standardised psychological stressors such as the Trier Social Stress Test produce measurable changes in ACTH and cortisol, and ACTH is one of the biomarkers examined in systematic reviews of chronic stress.[10][4]

In the adrenal cortex, MC2R activation raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A. Within minutes this increases cholesterol delivery to the mitochondria, and over hours it increases transcription of steroid-making enzymes, producing cortisol from the zona fasciculata and androgens from the zona reticularis.[1] MC2R is also expressed in bone-forming osteoblasts.[1] Cloning of the melanocortin receptor family in 1992 clarified how ACTH and the MSH peptides act on different tissues.[11]

Alpha-MSH, which shares its amino-terminal sequence with ACTH, stimulates melanin production in skin.[1] A major review describes the hormonal regulation of mammalian skin pigmentation, including the role of POMC products.[12] In Addison's disease, low cortisol leaves ACTH chronically high, and darkened skin is a recognised sign.[1]

sections.h: ACTH in hormone disorders that affect appearance
paras: Cushing's syndrome is caused by prolonged exposure to excess glucocorticoid, either from an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour (Cushing's disease), an ectopic ACTH source, an adrenal tumour or glucocorticoid medication. Reviews describe a constellation of signs and symptoms with multisystem effects, including changes to metabolism, skin and body fat, and note that diagnosis is often delayed by years because the features overlap with common conditions.[2][3]

Low ACTH occurs in hypopituitarism, where ACTH deficiency causes cortisol deficiency, and high ACTH occurs in primary adrenal insufficiency.[13][1] Clinicians use morning cortisol, ACTH and stimulation testing to tell these apart.[13][1]

Appearance signs of ACTH-driven cortisol excess are well catalogued. Wikipedia's description of Cushing's syndrome lists a rounded, flushed face, central weight gain with thin limbs, fat pads above the collarbones and at the back of the neck, thin skin that bruises easily, purple or red stretch marks, acne, and in some people excess facial hair or hair thinning.[14] About 70 percent of endogenous cases are Cushing's disease, an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumour, while the most common cause overall is glucocorticoid medication such as prednisone.[14] In the ACTH-independent forms caused by an adrenal tumour, ACTH is low and skin darkening does not develop, because the pigment-stimulating peptide is made together with ACTH.[14]

In Addison's disease, first described by Thomas Addison in 1855, ACTH and alpha-MSH rise because low cortisol removes the brake on the pituitary. Darkening appears in sun-exposed and unexposed skin, especially skin creases, palm lines, the nipples, the inside of the cheek and old scars.[15] Secondary and tertiary adrenal insufficiency do not cause this darkening, since ACTH is not overproduced in them.[15] These conditions are treated by physicians with hormone replacement or by treating the underlying tumour, and the visible signs are managed as part of that care.[14][15]

Corticotropin from pig pituitaries and the synthetic fragment tetracosactide (the first 24 amino acids, also called cosyntropin or Synacthen) are both used in the ACTH stimulation test of adrenal function, in which healthy adrenals raise blood cortisol within about 30 minutes of a dose.[5] In the United States the therapeutic gel is approved for infantile spasms, multiple sclerosis relapses and a range of rheumatic, inflammatory, skin, eye and kidney conditions.[5] The US tetracosactide label covers diagnosis, while the UK label also allows short-term therapeutic use where glucocorticoids are unsuitable.[5]

Registered trials include ACTH for relapsing nephrotic syndrome (n=31, phase 3),[6] diabetic nephropathy proteinuria,[16] multiple sclerosis myelination and fatigue,[7][17] uveitis[8] and rheumatoid arthritis with methotrexate.[9] These are small studies in patients with specific diseases. No published trials have tested ACTH for cosmetic or physique goals.

Because ACTH raises cortisol, prolonged exposure can produce features seen in Cushing's syndrome, including weight gain, skin thinning and mood changes.[2] Product labels and reviews list higher infection risk, suppression of the HPA axis and Cushing's syndrome among the effects, with contraindications that vary by country.[5] Medicinal corticotropin is dispensed under medical supervision.

The adrenotropic activity of the pituitary was characterised in the early 1930s. Wikipedia credits Evelyn Anderson with James Collip and David Thomson as co-discoverers, with a 1933 paper describing the hormone's function.[1] Klaus Hofmann at the University of Pittsburgh later made the first active synthetic fragment, and shorter synthetic peptides such as tetracosactide followed.[1] Wikipedia also notes that Semax, a Russian peptide, is a synthetic analogue built from a fragment of ACTH.[1]

The US price of Acthar Gel rose from about 40 dollars a vial in 2001 to roughly 28,000 dollars by 2013 after it was acquired first by Questcor and then Mallinckrodt. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general sued over anticompetitive conduct, and Mallinckrodt settled in January 2017, agreeing to pay 100 million dollars.[5] In Canada the price of Synacthen Depot reportedly rose by about 2,000 percent in 2015, and some provinces delisted it.[5]

Wikipedia notes that professional cyclists have reportedly used tetracosactide to raise glucocorticoid secretion.[5] On T Nation, ACTH appears mostly in threads where men on testosterone therapy discuss bloodwork: users post ACTH and morning cortisol results when trying to work out whether adrenal or pituitary function explains fatigue or low libido, and others reply that adrenal insufficiency cannot be diagnosed without such labs.[18][19]

lore.intro: ACTH is discussed in bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation forums as a lab marker rather than as something people take.[18][19]
